explanation:
## The program

```cpp
long long n{};
int steps{};

while (n != 1)
{
    if (n % 2 == 0) n /= 2;
    else            n = 3 * n + 1;
    ++steps;
}
```

## A loop with no count

```
6 → 3 → 10 → 5 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1        8 steps
7 → 22 → 11 → 34 → 17 → 52 → … → 1          16 steps
27 → 82 → 41 → 124 → … (up to 9232) → 1    111 steps
```

There is no formula for the length, and no way to pick a `for`
bound. The loop ends because the value happens to reach 1, which is
the defining feature of a `while`: the data decides.

It is also, famously, not *proved* to end for every starting value.
The Collatz conjecture is open; it has been checked by machine past
2⁶⁸, which covers this exercise several times over, and nobody has
a proof. A loop that might not terminate is normally a bug — here it
is an unsolved problem, which is a nice reminder that "this loop
ends" is a claim and not a formality.

## Why long long

The sequence does not decrease monotonically. From 27 it rises to
9232; from 704,511 it rises past 5.6 × 10¹⁰. A 32-bit `int` holds
up to about 2.1 × 10⁹, so `3 * n + 1` overflows well before then.

Signed integer overflow in C++ is undefined behaviour. Not "wraps to
a negative number" — although that is what usually happens, and it
would send the loop off somewhere strange. The compiler is allowed
to assume it never occurs, which means an optimiser can reason that
`n` is always positive and transform the loop on that basis. There
is no safe reading of a program that overflows.

`long long` is at least 64 bits by the standard — in practice
exactly 64 — which holds about 9.2 × 10¹⁸.

Note that the counter stays an `int`. Widening everything "to be
safe" is a habit worth not forming; widen the thing that can
actually get large, and know why.

## Zero steps is an answer

With `n == 1` the condition is false before the first pass and the
count is 0. As with the digit-reversal problem, an empty loop gives
the right answer because the accumulator started at the identity —
and a special case for it would be noise.

## What this does not check

Starting values outside 1 to 1,000,000. Zero loops forever (`0 / 2`
is 0), and a negative start falls into one of the known negative
cycles and never reaches 1. The constraint is doing real work, and a
program taking this from a user would have to check it rather than
hang.
